Planning a step-by-step guide to building an API project.

Planning a step-by-step guide to building an API project.

Done

Let's build this together. You have about nine days until the Oct 6 deadline, which is enough time if we keep a steady pace.

One thing first: the course's LLM policy says you must submit the chat logs from any AI you used and answer a survey about it. That includes this conversation, so save the link.

The roadmap

Here's the path we'll follow. We'll finish each step, and you'll understand it, before moving to the next.

Choose an API and explore its data. Everything else depends on this.

Set up the repo and deploy a blank app. Deploying early means the tricky base/basename setup is solved before it can go wrong at 11 PM on the due date.

Model the data in TypeScript and build an API layer with Axios.

Build the routing skeleton with React Router, with empty pages for List, Gallery, and Detail.

List view: search as you type, sort by two or more properties, ascending and descending.

Gallery view: images plus a multi-select attribute filter.

Detail view: its own URL, plus working Previous and Next buttons.

Design polish, final deploy, and the demo video.

Step 1: Choosing your API

This decision matters more than it looks, because the rubric asks for specific things from your data. Before picking, check that your API has:

A way to get a list of items. This feeds your search and list view.

At least two sortable properties per item, like name plus a number such as ID, rating, or year.

An image for each item. This feeds the gallery.

A categorical attribute with several values, like genre or type. This drives the gallery filter, where an item can match one or many.

Stable IDs, so a URL like /pokemon/25 always shows the same item.

Here's how a few of the options stack up:

PokéAPI needs no key, and every Pokémon has a sprite, a type (a great filter), and numeric stats (easy sorting). Its catch is that it can't search by partial name. That's fine here, though, because the assignment allows client-side filtering. You'd fetch something like the first 151 Pokémon and filter them yourself. This one is the most beginner-friendly.

TMDB gives you rich data: posters, genres, ratings, release dates, and a real search endpoint. It needs a free API key, and that key will be visible in your public repo. That's allowed since the key is free, but it's something you should understand.

TheMealDB needs no key and has nice food photos, with categories and cuisines to filter on. Its weakness is that it has few numeric properties, so meeting the "sort by 2 properties" requirement takes a bit more creativity.

Art Institute of Chicago needs no key and has beautiful images, but its image URLs require assembling a special format (IIIF), which adds a small hurdle.

Your task: pick one. Then spend five minutes opening a couple of its endpoints in your browser, for example https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/pokemon/pikachu. Look at the JSON and find the fields you'd use for sorting, the image, and the filter.

Reply with your choice and the fields you spotted, plus a line on how comfortable you are with React and TypeScript so far, so I can pitch my explanations at the right level. Then we'll move on to Step 2.

Unfortunately, the Marvel API no longer works. Marvel retired its developer portal in late 2025, and the portal no longer issues keys, while the server that hosted the API returns errors instead of data. There's no key you can get, so it's not an option.

If Marvel characters are what drew you in, though, there's a good alternative.

Option A: the SuperHero API (the closest substitute)

This is a free, open dataset of about 700 heroes and villains, many of them from Marvel. It needs no key or sign-up, and there's no rate limit, because it's just JSON files hosted on GitHub. The assignment explicitly allows APIs beyond its list, so this is fair game.

Here's how it maps onto the rubric. I pulled one character to check:

List view and search: one URL returns every hero, which you search by name.

Sorting by 2+ properties: each hero has name plus numeric powerstats (intelligence, strength, speed, durability, power, and combat).

Gallery images: every hero has images in four sizes (xs, sm, md, lg).

Gallery filter (select one or many): biography.publisher (Marvel Comics, DC Comics, and so on), biography.alignment (good, bad, or neutral), or appearance.gender.

Detail view with a URL: each hero has a numeric id, so a URL like /hero/1 works naturally.

You could even make it Marvel-only by keeping just the characters whose publisher is "Marvel Comics".

Option B: PokéAPI (the gentlest for a first React project)

It has well-documented, very popular data, with lots of examples online. The data is slightly more nested, and you'd make one request per Pokémon for details.

My recommendation

Since this is your first time with React and TypeScript, I'd go with SuperHero API. You get the Marvel theme you wanted, and the data is simpler to work with. With one request you have the whole dataset, so you can focus on learning React instead of juggling API calls.

No, unfortunately that repo won't work.

That repo is a catalog entry about the Marvel API, not the API itself. It contains a description of the API (an OpenAPI spec), links, and a rating, but no actual character data. Its own README says it doesn't operate or host Marvel's API. Every link in it points back to the same retired endpoint, gateway.marvel.com, which no longer returns data. It also still requires a Marvel API key, which you can no longer get.

This is a useful distinction to learn early:

An API spec (OpenAPI, Postman collection) is like a restaurant's menu. It tells you what you could order and in what format.

A live API is the kitchen. It actually hands you the data when you send a request.

For your app you need a working kitchen. A menu for a restaurant that has closed can't feed you.

What to do instead

If you want Marvel characters, the SuperHero API is still your best bet. It's a live, working source that serves real character data and images, and you can filter it down to only Marvel characters. Try opening https://akabab.github.io/superhero-api/api/id/346.json in your browser; you'll see Iron Man's full data, which proves the kitchen is open.

When you're evaluating any API in the future, the quick test is to find one real request URL and open it. If you get back JSON with actual data, it's live. If you get an error, or only documentation, keep looking.

So: do you want to go with the SuperHero API (Marvel-only if you like), or pick something else? Once you choose, we'll move on to setting up your project.

Yes, this one works. It's the YGOPRODeck API, and it's live and free with no key needed. It's also a good fit for the rubric:

List view and search: each card has a name to search by.

Sorting by 2+ properties: name, atk (attack), def (defense), and level.

Gallery images: every card has a card_images array with full-size and small versions.

Gallery filter (one or many): attribute (DARK, LIGHT, FIRE, WATER, and so on), race (Dragon, Spellcaster, Warrior, and so on), or type (Effect Monster, Spell Card, and so on).

Detail view with a URL: each card has a numeric id, so a URL like /card/46986414 works.

Three rules this API comes with

Their docs spell these out, and they'll shape how we build.

Don't hotlink their images. They ask you to download card images once and host them yourself. If you keep pulling images from their server, your IP address gets blacklisted.

Rate limit: 20 requests per second. If you go over, you're blocked for an hour.

Store the data you fetch rather than re-requesting it constantly.

These rules push us toward a sensible plan. The full database has over 13,000 cards, which is far too many images to host. So we'll pick one card set, maybe around 100 cards. We'll download those images once into your project, and fetch the card data with Axios. The assignment even mentions caching and rate limits, so handling this well is part of the lesson.

A good candidate is Legend of Blue Eyes White Dragon, the original 2002 set, with classics like Dark Magician and Blue-Eyes. If you have a favorite set or archetype (Blue-Eyes, Dark Magician, Elemental HERO...), that works too.

Your task

Open this URL in your browser. It's a single request, so it's safe:

https://db.ygoprodeck.com/api/v7/cardinfo.php?name=Dark%20Magician

Look at the JSON and notice two things:

The card isn't at the top level. It's inside a data array. Why do you think the API wraps results in a list even when you ask for one card?

Find the card_images field. It's an array, not a single URL. Why might a card have more than one image?

Yes, NASA works, and it's a safe pick because it's on the assignment's own list of approved APIs. "NASA" is actually a collection of many APIs, though, so the real question is which one. For this assignment, I'd use the NASA Image and Video Library (images-api.nasa.gov). It needs no API key, it's built around images, and its fields map neatly onto the rubric.

How it fits the rubric

Each result comes with these fields: center (the NASA center which published the media), title, photographer, keywords, nasa_id, date_created, media_type, and description, plus preview image links.

List view and search: title.

Sorting by 2+ properties: title (A–Z) and date_created (oldest or newest).

Gallery images: the preview image link on each item.

Gallery filter (one or many): center, the NASA center that published it (like JSC or KSC). keywords would also work.

Detail view with a URL: nasa_id, giving URLs like /item/as11-40-5874.

Two things to know up front

Some fields are optional. Only nasa_id, title, media_type, center, and date_created are always present. That's why I suggested center for the filter instead of keywords: it's always there. Your code will still need to handle missing descriptions gracefully, which TypeScript is good at reminding you about.

Search vs. filter as you type. The API has a search endpoint, but the rubric wants filtering as you type. Sending a request on every keystroke would be slow and wasteful. So we'll fetch a themed batch once, like "apollo" or "mars" images, then filter and sort that list in the browser. The assignment explicitly allows client-side filtering.

Reviewing the structure of an astronomy data API.

Done

Yes, APOD works too. It's part of NASA's API collection, so it's covered by the assignment's approved list. It has one weak spot you should know about before choosing it.

How it fits the rubric

Each day's entry has date, title, explanation, url (the image), hdurl, media_type, and sometimes copyright.

List view and search: title works well.

Sorting by 2+ properties: title and date work well.

Gallery images: url works well, but some days are videos, not images.

Detail view with a URL: date works very well, giving URLs like /apod/2026-09-15. Previous and Next become "the day before" and "the day after," which feels natural.

Gallery filter (one or many): this is the weak spot.

The weak spot: APOD entries don't have a real category like "genre" or "type." The fields you could filter on are media_type (image or video), whether it has a copyright credit, or the year or month derived from the date. Filtering by month ("show me January and March") is a legitimate multi-select filter and would satisfy the rubric. It just takes a bit more work, because you compute the category yourself instead of reading it straight from the data.

Practical details

You'll need a free API key. You sign up at api.nasa.gov with just your email. There's a shared DEMO_KEY for testing, but it's heavily rate-limited, so use your own. Your key will be visible in your public repo. That's allowed since it's free, but it's worth knowing.

You can fetch many days in one request with start_date and end_date. So you'd load, say, the last 60 days once, then search and sort in the browser.

Compared to the Image and Video Library

APOD: a better detail view (beautiful explanations, date-based URLs), but a weaker filter.

Image Library: a natural built-in filter (center), no key needed, but messier nested JSON.

Both would get you full marks. It comes down to which data you'd enjoy looking at for the next nine days.

Your task

Open this in your browser:

https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod?api_key=DEMO_KEY&start_date=2026-09-01&end_date=2026-09-10

Notice that the response is an array of days, and compare how flat it is to the Image Library's nested structure. Check whether any of those ten days is a video instead of an image.

Planning a beginner-friendly walkthrough of React and TypeScript basics.

Planning a beginner-friendly walkthrough of React and TypeScript basics.

Done

APOD it is.

Step 2, part 1: The big picture, then your tools

Before touching any code, here's what each tool in this assignment actually does.

JavaScript is the language web browsers run. Every interactive website uses it.

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components. A component is a reusable piece of UI, written as a function that takes in data and returns what should appear on screen. Your app might have:

a SearchBar component

a PictureCard component (one APOD entry)

a Gallery component that displays many PictureCards

The key idea in React is that the UI is a function of your data. You don't manually say "add this element, remove that one." You say "here's the list of pictures; show them," and when the data changes (like the user typing in the search bar), React updates the screen for you.

TypeScript is JavaScript with types added. In plain JavaScript you could accidentally write picture.titel (a typo), and you'd only discover the bug when the page breaks. In TypeScript, you first describe what an APOD entry looks like:

interface ApodPicture {
  date: string;
  title: string;
  url: string;
}

Then your editor underlines picture.titel in red before you even run the code. It's like spell-check for your data.

Vite is the build tool. It creates your starter project, runs a local development server that refreshes instantly when you save a file, and bundles everything into plain files for deployment.

npm is the package manager. It downloads libraries others have written (React Router, Axios) into your project.

React Router lets your single-page app have multiple "pages" with real URLs like /gallery or /apod/2026-09-15, without reloading the browser.

Axios is a library for making requests to APIs, like fetching the pictures from NASA.

Your tasks for this part

These are all setup; no coding yet.

Get your NASA API key. Go to api.nasa.gov, fill in the form (name and email), and the key arrives by email. Keep it somewhere handy.

Check your tools. Open a terminal (Terminal on Mac, PowerShell on Windows) and run these three commands one at a time:
node -v
npm -v
git --version

Each should print a version number. If any says "command not found," that's fine, just tell me which one.

Create your repo. Follow submission step 1 in the assignment: open the class repo on GitHub, click Use this template → Create a new repository, name it mp2, and make it public. Don't clone it yet.

Reply with the three version numbers (or errors), and whether you got the key and created the repo. Then we'll clone the repo and generate your React project.

If you see a question with options, like "Current directory is not empty..." with choices listed underneath, it's waiting for your answer. These menus don't accept typed commands. 9/27/2026 20:08:30 Explaining why React state updates don't reflect immediately. Explaining why React state updates don't reflect immediately. Done You got all three right. Your third answer, "calling setCount() updates the state," is correct, but the reason behind it is the key to all of React, so here it is. Why setCount and not count = count + 1 A React component is a function, and React calls that function every time it needs to redraw that part of the screen. Each call is called a render. That creates a problem for normal variables. Imagine App had this: let count = 0; Every time App re-runs, that line runs again and count goes back to 0. Normal variables don't survive between renders. useState solves this. It asks React to keep a value in memory for this component across renders: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); 0 is the starting value, used only on the very first render. count is the current value React remembers. setCount is the function that changes that value. Calling setCount(count + 1) does two things: it stores the new value, and it tells React to re-render the component. React calls App again, useState hands back the new count, and the screen shows the new number. If you wrote count = count + 1 instead, the variable would change, but React would never find out, so it would never redraw. The screen would be stuck on the old number. The rule: any data that should change what's on screen goes in state, and you change it only through its setter. Why this matters for your app Your whole list view is built from state: Search text: a string in state that updates on every keystroke. Sort field: state, either "title" or "date". Sort order: state, either "asc" or "desc". The fetched pictures: state, starting empty and filled when the API responds. On each render, your component combines them: take the pictures, keep the ones whose title matches the search text, sort them, and display them. When any of these values changes, React re-renders and the list updates automatically. That's how "filter as you type" works, and it needs no special code. Your task: build a mini search box This is practice for the real search bar. It's throwaway code, so experiment freely. Step 3: Install libraries and connect to NASA

3a. Install Axios and React Router

In a second terminal inside mp2 (leave the dev server running), run:

npm install axios react-router

This downloads both libraries into node_modules and records them in package.json. That's how GitHub's deploy workflow knows to install them too. (In current versions of React Router, the package is just react-router; you'll see older tutorials use react-router-dom.)

3b. Create this folder structure

In src/, create these empty files:

src/
  types.ts           ← the TypeScript description of an APOD entry
  api/
    apod.ts          ← the function that calls NASA
  pages/
    ListView.tsx
    GalleryView.tsx
    DetailView.tsx

Splitting code like this keeps things findable: pages are what the user navigates to, api/ is how data gets fetched, and types.ts is shared by everything.

3c. Write the ApodPicture type (your job)

In types.ts, write an exported interface describing one APOD entry. Think back to the JSON from that URL you opened earlier. You need these fields:

date, title, explanation, url, hdurl, media_type, copyright, thumbnail_url

Two things to figure out:

Some fields aren't always present. copyright only appears when an image isn't public domain, hdurl is missing on videos, and thumbnail_url only appears on videos. In TypeScript, you mark a field as optional with a ? after its name: hdurl?: string;

media_type is only ever "image" or "video". You could type it as string, but TypeScript lets you be stricter: media_type: 'image' | 'video';. That means it must be exactly one of those two values. The | means "or."

Start it like this and fill in the rest:

export interface ApodPicture {
  date: string;
  // ...your fields here
}

export makes the interface usable from other files.

3d. The API function

Put this in api/apod.ts, then read the explanation below it:

import axios from 'axios';
import type { ApodPicture } from '../types';

const API_KEY = 'YOUR_KEY_HERE';
const BASE_URL = 'https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod';

export async function fetchPictures(startDate: string, endDate: string): Promise<ApodPicture[]> {
  const response = await axios.get<ApodPicture[]>(BASE_URL, {
    params: {
      api_key: API_KEY,
      start_date: startDate,
      end_date: endDate,
      thumbs: true,
    },
  });
  return response.data;
}

Here's what each part does:

async / await: a network request takes time. await pauses this function until NASA responds, without freezing the rest of the page. Any function that uses await must be marked async.

Promise<ApodPicture[]>: this is the return type. An async function returns a promise, meaning "a list of pictures, eventually."

axios.get<ApodPicture[]>: the <...> tells TypeScript what shape to expect back. From then on, response.data is typed as an array of your interface.

params: Axios builds the ?api_key=...&start_date=... part of the URL for you.

thumbs: true: asks NASA to include thumbnail_url for video entries, so your gallery can show an image for every entry, including videos.

Replace YOUR_KEY_HERE with your key. It will be public in your repo; that's acceptable for a free key, as the assignment notes.

Your types.ts once it's written. I'll check it, and then we'll call fetchPictures from a page and see real NASA data on your screen.

Step 6: Search and sort (the first 28 rubric points)

All of this happens inside ListView. The idea: keep the user's choices in state, then on every render, compute the list to display from pictures plus those choices.

6a. Three new pieces of state

Add these at the top of ListView (you'll need to import useState):

query: the search text, starting as ''.

sortField: which property to sort by. Type it as 'title' | 'date' and start with 'date'.

sortOrder: type it as 'asc' | 'desc' and start with 'desc', so newest comes first.

For the union types, pass the type explicitly: useState<'title' | 'date'>('date').

6b. The controls

Above your <ul>, add:

A text input for searching. Set value={query} and an onChange that calls setQuery(e.target.value). This is a controlled input: state is the source of truth, and the input just displays it. Since every keystroke updates state, and every state update re-renders the list, that's "filter as you type."

A <select> for the sort field, with two <option>s: value="title" and value="date". Wire it the same way: value={sortField} and an onChange that calls setSortField.

A <select> (or two buttons) for the order: ascending and descending.

You'll hit one TypeScript complaint with the selects: e.target.value is typed as a plain string, but setSortField only accepts 'title' | 'date'. TypeScript can't know your <option>s only contain those two values, but you do. So you tell it with a type assertion:

as means "trust me, it's this type." Use it only when you genuinely know better than TypeScript, like here.

Give each control a <label>. It's good design and good accessibility.

6c. Compute the displayed list

Between your state and the return, compute the list in two steps.

Filter. Use .filter() to keep pictures whose title contains the query. .filter() keeps an item when your function returns true. Make it case-insensitive, so "moon" finds "Moon": lowercase both sides with .toLowerCase(), then use .includes(). Try writing this one yourself.

Sort. Here's the structure, with the key part left for you:

const sorted = [...filtered].sort((a, b) => {
  const result = /* compare a and b by sortField */;
  return sortOrder === 'asc' ? result : -result;
});

Three things to understand here:

[...filtered] makes a copy. .sort() rearranges the array it's called on. The original pictures comes from App, and a component must never modify its props, so you sort a copy.

How .sort() works: it calls your function with pairs of items. Return a negative number if a goes first, positive if b goes first, and 0 if they're equal. Negating the result (-result) flips the order, which is how you get descending.

For the comparison, use localeCompare. For strings, a.title.localeCompare(b.title) returns exactly that negative/zero/positive number, and it handles alphabetical order properly. Since sortField holds the property name, you can write a[sortField].localeCompare(b[sortField]) to cover both cases in one line.

You might wonder how that works for dates. It works because APOD dates are formatted YYYY-MM-DD: biggest unit first, zero-padded. For that format, alphabetical order is chronological order. "2026-09-05" comes before "2026-09-15" either way. That's one reason this format is a standard.

If you get a GitHub "404 File not found" page, here's why and how to fix it.

Why it happens

Your app has only one real HTML file, index.html. The routes like /apod/2026-09-15 exist only inside React Router, which runs after index.html loads.

When you click a link inside the app, React Router handles it, and GitHub never sees the request. But when you refresh or paste a URL, the browser asks GitHub's server for /mp2/apod/2026-09-15. GitHub looks for a file at that path, finds none, and returns its 404 page. Your app never gets a chance to load.

The rubric requires that "a user should be able to access the detail route through a specific url," so this matters for points.

The fix

When GitHub Pages can't find a file, it serves a file named 404.html if one exists. So if 404.html is simply a copy of index.html, any unknown URL loads your app, and React Router then reads the URL and shows the right page.

In package.json, find the "build" line under "scripts". It looks something like:

"build": "tsc -b && vite build",

Add a copy command to the end:

"build": "tsc -b && vite build && cp dist/index.html dist/404.html",

&& means "then, if the previous command succeeded, run the next one."

vite build produces your deployable site in dist/.

cp dist/index.html dist/404.html makes the copy. The deploy workflow runs this build script on GitHub's servers, so the copy happens automatically on every push.

Keep whatever your existing build line has before the &&; just append the copy command.

Test

Calculating the date range needed to cover several months.

Calculating the date range needed to cover several months.

Done

Only three months show because of the date range you fetch. In App.tsx, the app asks NASA for the last 60 days:

start.setDate(start.getDate() - 60);

Today is September 28, so 60 days back is July 30. That range covers only three months: a couple of days of July, all of August, and September so far. The month buttons are built from whatever months appear in the data, so there are three.

This is also why the July button, if you have one, shows only a picture or two.

If you want more months

A cleaner approach is to fetch whole months, so none of them are partial. Replace the two date lines in App.tsx with:

const start = new Date();
start.setDate(1);
start.setMonth(start.getMonth() - 5);

This moves to the 1st of the current month, then goes back 5 months. That's April 1 through today: six full months, with six filter buttons.

The order of those two lines matters. JavaScript "rolls over" impossible dates. If today were March 31 and you went back one month first, you'd get "February 31," which JavaScript silently turns into March 3, and you'd barely move at all. Setting the day to the 1st first means every month has that day, so the rollover can't happen.

Change the 5 to go further back. More months means more filter buttons and a longer list, but it's still a single request, so the rate limit isn't a concern. Around 6 months (about 180 pictures) is a good size: plenty of variety, and it still loads quickly.

Here's what each item does, grouped by role.

Your app's code: src/

This is where everything you wrote lives.

main.tsx: the entry point, the first code that runs. It loads Normalize.css and your global styles, wraps the app in BrowserRouter (with the /mp2/ basename), and renders App into the page.

App.tsx: the top-level component. It fetches the APOD data once from NASA, holds the pictures, loading, and error state, renders the header and nav, and defines the three routes, passing the data down to each page.

App.module.css: styles for the header, nav links (including the highlighted active tab), main layout, and loading and error messages.

index.css: global styles for the whole app: the color variables (--bg, --accent, and so on), fonts, and body background. It's the only non-module stylesheet.

types.ts: TypeScript shapes shared across files: ApodPicture (one APOD entry) and DetailNavState (the ordered list of dates passed to the detail page).

utils.ts: small shared helpers:
getImageUrl: picks the best image for an entry.

getYouTubeThumbnail: builds a YouTube thumbnail URL.

isVideoFile: detects .mp4 and similar files.

formatMonth: turns "2026-09" into "September 2026."

api/apod.ts: the only file that talks to NASA. fetchPictures uses Axios to request APOD entries from a start date to today, with your API key and thumbs: true.

pages/ListView.tsx and its CSS module: the list page. It handles search-as-you-type, the type filter, and sorting by title or date in either order. Each row links to the detail page, sending along the visible sequence.

pages/GalleryView.tsx and its CSS module: the gallery page. It shows a responsive grid of tiles, with toggleable Month and Type filters that combine. Each tile links to the detail page, also sending the visible sequence.

pages/DetailView.tsx and its CSS module: the detail page. It reads the date from the URL, shows the picture or an embedded video with its title, date, copyright, and explanation, and provides Previous and Next buttons that follow the sequence you came from (or all pictures, for direct URLs).

components/Thumbnail.tsx and its CSS module: the shared tile used by both the list and gallery. It shows an image, a video thumbnail, a video frame, or a placeholder, with lazy loading.

The web page and settings

index.html: the single HTML page of your single-page app. It contains the browser tab title, the icon, and an empty <div id="root"> that React fills in.

vite.config.ts: Vite's settings. The important line is base: '/mp2/', which tells the built site where it lives on GitHub Pages.

package.json: the project's manifest. It lists your dependencies (React, React Router, Axios, Normalize.css) and scripts (dev, build with the 404.html copy, and lint).

package-lock.json: records the exact version of every installed package, so GitHub's deploy installs exactly what you tested with. It's required by the workflow's npm ci. Never edit it by hand.

tsconfig.json, tsconfig.app.json, tsconfig.node.json: TypeScript settings. app covers your code in src/, node covers config files like vite.config.ts, and tsconfig.json ties the two together. You haven't needed to change them.

.oxlintrc.json: settings for Oxlint, the linter that npm run lint runs.

Git and deployment

.git/: git's hidden database, containing your entire commit history. Never edit or delete it.

.gitignore: tells git which files not to track, such as node_modules and dist.

.github/: contains workflows/deploy.yml, the automated pipeline from the class template. On every push to main, GitHub installs your dependencies, runs npm run build, and publishes the result to GitHub Pages.

README.md: the class's README. You'll add your live URL and Sources section here.

Generated or downloaded (not your code)

node_modules/: the downloaded library code, often hundreds of megabytes. It's ignored by git and can always be recreated with npm install.

dist/: the output of npm run build, the actual files deployed: minified JavaScript, CSS, index.html, and 404.html. It's recreated on every build, and GitHub builds its own copy when deploying.

public/: files copied into the build as-is. It may only hold vite.svg now; if you switched to the emoji icon, you can delete it.

Two things to check

.DS_Store is a hidden file macOS creates in folders to remember view settings. It has nothing to do with your project and shouldn't be in the repo. Check whether git is tracking it by running git ls-files .DS_Store. If that prints the filename, remove it from the repo and ignore it from now on:
git rm --cached .DS_Store
echo ".DS_Store" >> .gitignore

--cached removes it from git only, not from your disk. >> appends a line to the end of .gitignore.

dist should be listed in .gitignore. Vite's template includes it, but confirm by opening .gitignore and looking for a dist line. If it's missing, add it, the same way as above.

If either check needed a change, commit and push afterward.

Yes. TypeScript runs through the whole project, in two ways: every code file is written in it, and it's enforced at build time.

It's in every code file, and it's enforced

Every code file is .ts or .tsx, not .js or .jsx.

Your build script starts with tsc -b, the TypeScript compiler. It checks every type in the project before Vite bundles anything. If there were a type error, npm run build would stop, and GitHub's deploy would fail. So your live site is proof that the code type-checks.

Where you used it, file by file

Describing your data (types.ts)

The ApodPicture interface describes an APOD entry. It uses optional fields (hdurl?, copyright?, thumbnail_url?) and a union type (media_type: 'image' | 'video').

DetailNavState describes the data passed to the detail page.

Typing the API call (api/apod.ts)

axios.get<ApodPicture[]> tells TypeScript what NASA sends back, so response.data is typed.

Promise<ApodPicture[]> is the function's return type.

Typing component props (every page)

ListViewProps, GalleryViewProps, DetailViewProps, and ThumbnailProps define what each component requires. Earlier, when you wrote <ListView /> without pictures, TypeScript flagged it right away.

Typing state

useState<ApodPicture[]>([]), useState<string | null>(null)

Union types restrict state to specific values: useState<'title' | 'date'>, useState<'asc' | 'desc'>, useState<'all' | 'image' | 'video'>, useState<('image' | 'video')[]>

Typed function signatures (utils.ts)

For example, getImageUrl(picture: ApodPicture): string | undefined. The | undefined forced you to handle pictures with no image, which is why the gallery tiles have fallbacks instead of breaking.

More advanced features

Type assertions: e.target.value as 'title' | 'date' in the dropdowns, and location.state as DetailNavState | null in DetailView.

A generic function: toggle<T>(list: T[], value: T): T[] in the gallery, one function that works for both month strings and media types.

as const: ['image', 'video'] as const, so the button values are typed as the exact literals rather than plain strings.

import type: type-only imports, like import type { ApodPicture } from '../types', which are removed entirely from the final JavaScript.

Where TypeScript caught real bugs

Some examples from this build:

It flagged <ListView /> missing its required pictures prop.

It flagged NavLink as "Cannot find name" when the import was missing.

It would reject setSortField('titel'), a typo, because only 'title' or 'date' are allowed.

Worth remembering from earlier: import.meta.env.mp2 was the one bug TypeScript couldn't catch, because Vite types that object loosely. TypeScript catches a lot, but not everything.

If a grader asks, or you want to mention it in your demo video, the short version is: "Every file is TypeScript. The data, props, state, and API responses are all typed, and the build runs the TypeScript compiler, so the deployed site type-checks."

Explaining React components and their structure.

Explaining React components and their structure.

Done

A React component is a function, named with a capital letter, that takes props as input and returns JSX describing what to show. Your app is a tree of these components, each one rendering the ones below it.

The component tree

StrictMode                         (React, main.tsx)
└─ BrowserRouter                   (React Router, main.tsx)
   └─ App                          (yours, App.tsx)
      ├─ Link                      (brand title → home)
      ├─ NavLink ×2                (List / Gallery tabs)
      └─ Routes
         ├─ Route "/"          → ListView
         │                        ├─ Thumbnail   (one per row)
         │                        └─ Link        (one per row → detail)
         ├─ Route "/gallery"   → GalleryView
         │                        ├─ Thumbnail   (one per tile)
         │                        └─ Link        (one per tile → detail)
         └─ Route "/apod/:date"→ DetailView
                                  └─ Link ×2     (Previous / Next)

Only one of the three pages is rendered at a time. Routes picks the Route whose path matches the current URL.

Your own components (5)

App (App.tsx)

Rendered by: main.tsx, inside BrowserRouter.

Props: none. It's the top of your tree.

Job: fetches the data, holds pictures, loading, and error, renders the header and nav, and decides which page to show.

ListView (pages/ListView.tsx)

Rendered by: App, through <Route path="/" element={<ListView pictures={pictures} />} />

Props: pictures

Job: its own state for search, type filter, and sorting; renders the controls and one row per visible picture.

GalleryView (pages/GalleryView.tsx)

Rendered by: App, on /gallery.

Props: pictures

Job: its own state for selected months and types; renders the filter buttons and one tile per visible picture.

DetailView (pages/DetailView.tsx)

Rendered by: App, on /apod/:date.

Props: pictures and loading

Job: finds the picture from the URL, shows it, and links to the previous and next entries in the sequence.

Thumbnail (components/Thumbnail.tsx)

Rendered by: ListView (inside each row) and GalleryView (inside each tile). This is your one reusable component.

Props: picture, plus an optional className.

Job: decides between an image, a video frame, or a placeholder. The parent controls the size through className: 72px squares in the list, full grid squares in the gallery. Same component, two different looks.

Library components you used

From React: StrictMode (development checks) and fragments <> </> (invisible grouping).

From React Router: BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link, and NavLink.

You use them exactly like your own components, as tags with props. For example, <Link to="/gallery"> passes the prop to, the same way <Thumbnail picture={picture} /> passes picture.

The patterns

Pages vs. components: pages (in pages/) are what routes display. Components (in components/) are building blocks used inside pages.

Data flows down through props: App → pages → Thumbnail. A child never changes its props; it only reads them.

State lives where it's needed:
pictures is in App because all three pages share it.

query and sortField are in ListView because only the list uses them.

selectedMonths is in GalleryView.

Every component is typed: each has a props interface (ListViewProps, ThumbnailProps, and so on), so TypeScript checks every place a component is used.

Reuse over duplication: Thumbnail replaced the gallery's renderTile function the moment the list needed the same logic.

One component per file, each with its own .module.css, so styles can't leak between components.

These are arrays because the gallery allows selecting several options at once.

How state flows: user action → state → screen

Take typing "moon" in the search box:

The input's onChange fires on each keystroke and calls setQuery('moon').

React stores the new value and re-runs ListView.

This time query is 'moon', so filtered, then sorted, then navState are recomputed from it.

The JSX maps over the new sorted, and React updates only the rows that changed.

Every control in the app follows this same loop.

The rules you followed

Only change state through its setter. A plain assignment like query = 'moon' would change the variable, but React would never find out, so it would never re-render.

Never modify state in place. Always make a new value. toggle returns a new array, using .filter() to remove or [...list, value] to add. It never calls .push() on the existing one. React decides whether to re-render by checking whether it got a new value. An array changed in place looks like the "same array," so the update would be skipped. The same thinking is behind [...filtered].sort(): .sort() rearranges the array it's called on, so you sort a copy.

Store the minimum; compute the rest. filtered, sorted, visible, months, hasFilters, and navState are not state. They're derived from state and props on every render. If you stored sorted in state too, you'd have to remember to update it every time the query, filter, or sort changed. Deriving it means it can never be out of sync.

Controlled inputs. Each input and dropdown takes its value from state and reports changes back through onChange. State is the single source of truth, and the input only displays it.

Keep state where it's used. pictures is in App because all pages share it. The search and sort choices are in ListView because nothing else needs them. One side effect: your list filters reset when you navigate away and come back, because ListView is removed from the screen and its state goes with it.

Related, but not React state

Two other things act like state but are owned by React Router, not useState:

The URL (/apod/:date, read with useParams) decides which picture DetailView shows. Putting it in the URL is what makes the detail page bookmarkable and shareable.

Navigation state (DetailNavState, read with useLocation) is the filtered sequence carried from the list or gallery to the detail page. It's attached to the browser's history entry, which is why it survives a refresh.

Explaining React Router setup and navigation features.

Explaining React Router setup and navigation features.

Done

React Router turns your single page into an app with multiple URLs. It watches the browser's address bar and decides which component to show, all without reloading the page. It comes from the react-router package you installed in Step 3.

1. Connecting to the browser: BrowserRouter (main.tsx)

<BrowserRouter basename={import.meta.env.BASE_URL}>
  <App />
</BrowserRouter>

It wraps your whole app, so every component inside can read or change the URL.

basename is /mp2/, taken from base in vite.config.ts, because your site lives at username.github.io/mp2/, not at the root. Every route and link is automatically relative to /mp2/.

2. Mapping URLs to pages: Routes and Route (App.tsx)

<Routes>
  <Route path="/" element={<ListView pictures={pictures} />} />
  <Route path="/gallery" element={<GalleryView pictures={pictures} />} />
  <Route path="/apod/:date" element={<DetailView pictures={pictures} loading={loading} />} />
</Routes>

URL
Shows
/mp2/
ListView
/mp2/gallery
GalleryView
/mp2/apod/2026-09-15
DetailView for that date

Routes renders only the one Route that matches the current URL.

:date is a URL parameter, a placeholder that matches any value. It's what gives every picture its own address, as the rubric requires.

The header sits outside Routes, so it appears on every page.

3. Navigating: Link and NavLink

Link changes the URL without reloading the page. You used it in five places:

Where
Goes to
Header title (App)
/
Each list row (ListView)
/apod/<date>
Each gallery tile (GalleryView)
/apod/<date>
Previous and Next (DetailView)
/apod/<prev or next date>
"Back to the list" on the not-found message (DetailView)
/

A plain <a href> would make the browser request a new page from the server, which throws away all your state and the already-loaded data. Link intercepts the click, updates the URL, and lets Routes swap the component. It also adds the /mp2/ basename automatically, which is why the assignment says to use Link instead of <a>.

The one place you correctly used <a> is the external video link, because it leaves your app entirely.

NavLink is a Link that knows whether it's the current page. The List and Gallery tabs use it to highlight the active tab:

<NavLink to="/" end className={({ isActive }) => (isActive ? styles.activeLink : styles.link)}>

end makes the List tab active only on exactly /. Otherwise it would match every page, since every path starts with /.

4. Reading the URL: useParams (DetailView)

const { date } = useParams();

On /apod/2026-09-15, this gives date = "2026-09-15", which DetailView uses to find the picture. The URL itself is the input to the page.

5. Passing data between pages: state and useLocation

This is how the filtered order reaches the detail page.

Sending, in ListView and GalleryView:

<Link to={`/apod/${picture.date}`} state={navState}>

Receiving, in DetailView:

const location = useLocation();
const navState = location.state as DetailNavState | null;

state rides along with the navigation, invisible in the URL. It's the list of dates the user was looking at.

DetailView uses it for Previous and Next, and passes it forward on every step so it isn't lost.

If there's no state (for example, someone pasted the URL), it falls back to all pictures by date.

6. Making direct URLs work on GitHub Pages

This isn't React Router code, but it exists because of React Router. Your routes exist only inside the app, so GitHub's server has no file at /mp2/apod/2026-09-15 and would return a 404 on refresh. Your build copies index.html to 404.html, so GitHub serves your app for any unknown path, and React Router then reads the URL and shows the right page.

The whole flow in one example

Say you click a video in the gallery after filtering to Videos:

Link updates the URL to /mp2/apod/2026-09-10, attaching state with the video dates. No reload happens.

BrowserRouter notices the URL change, and Routes matches /apod/:date, so it renders DetailView.

useParams gives date, and useLocation gives the video sequence.

DetailView shows the video and builds Previous and Next links that carry the same state forward.

Investigating whether date parameters actually work as documented.

Read a page

Extracting embedded video links from the article's HTML content.

Done

The documentation says you can, but in practice the new endpoint ignores those parameters right now.

Can you request specific days?

The docs list date, start_date, end_date, and count, but I tested them directly against the new endpoint, and every one of these returned the same thing, the latest entries starting from today (October 1):

?date=2026-07-04

?start_date=2026-07-01&end_date=2026-07-05

?per_page=60

Other developers have hit the same wall. One reported that requesting a specific date from the new endpoint just returns a list of 25 entries, with count, date, start_date, and end_date all having no effect.

You can confirm it yourself: open https://science.nasa.gov/wp-json/wp/v2/apod-basic?date=2026-07-04 in your browser and look at the first "date". It will be today's, not July 4th.

This is a real-world lesson worth noting in your README: documentation describes what an API is supposed to do; testing tells you what it actually does. NASA may fix this later, but you can't rely on it before Oct 6. So the app shows the most recent 25 days, and that's the right call.

Why the 2 videos won't load

In the new API, a video entry's url is the link to NASA's article page, not the video itself. Our adapter puts that article URL into the <iframe>, and NASA's site refuses to be embedded inside other sites, so the frame stays blank. There's also no thumbnail, since thumbs is disabled.

The actual video link still exists, though. It's inside the basic_html field, which contains the full HTML of the old-style APOD page. A video page has an <iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/..."> (or a <video> tag for .mp4 files) somewhere in that HTML. We can parse the HTML and pull out that src, the same way htmlToText already parses HTML.

Section 1: Update api/apod.ts

1. Add basic_html to RawApodEntry:

basic_html?: string;

2. Add this function next to htmlToText:

function findVideoUrl(basicHtml: string | undefined): string | undefined {
  if (!basicHtml) return undefined;
  const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(basicHtml, 'text/html');
  const player = doc.querySelector('iframe[src], video[src], video source[src]');
  const src = player?.getAttribute('src');
  return src ? new URL(src, 'https://science.nasa.gov/').href : undefined;
}

Here's what each line does:

DOMParser turns the HTML string into a document you can search, the same as in htmlToText. Parsing doesn't run anything inside the HTML; we only read attributes.

querySelector finds the first element matching a CSS selector. The selector lists three possibilities, separated by commas:
iframe[src]: an iframe that has a src (YouTube or Vimeo embeds).

video[src]: a <video> tag with its file in src.

video source[src]: a <source> inside a <video>, the other common way to write a video tag.

player?.getAttribute('src') reads the link. The ?. handles the case where nothing matched.

new URL(src, 'https://science.nasa.gov/') turns relative links (like /apod/image/clip.mp4) or protocol-relative links (like //www.youtube.com/embed/...) into full URLs. If src is already a full URL, it's returned unchanged.

3. In toPicture, change the url line to:

url: isVideo ? (findVideoUrl(raw.basic_html) ?? raw.url) : (raw.hdurl ?? raw.url),

For videos, this uses the real video link if one is found, and falls back to the article page otherwise.

Section 2: Recognize more YouTube links (utils.ts)

YouTube embeds sometimes use the youtube-nocookie.com domain. Update the regex in getYouTubeThumbnail to accept both:

const match = url.match(/youtube(?:-nocookie)?\.com\/embed\/([\w-]+)/);

(?:-nocookie)? means "optionally the text -nocookie." The ?: makes it a group that isn't captured, so the video ID stays in match[1].

Once url holds the real YouTube embed link, your existing getImageUrl will build a thumbnail from it automatically, so the gallery tile shows a proper image.

Checking whether API calls need authentication to return data.

Done

Good questions. Here are both answers, plus one fix the new documentation reveals.

Could leaving out count be the problem?

No. count is opt-in: if you don't include it in the URL, you aren't using it. There's no need to say "don't use count." The rule "cannot be used with date" only matters when you send both in the same request, and in my tests I sent date alone, and start_date with end_date alone, without count. Both still returned the latest entries.

The server receives the parameters but doesn't act on them. Default to the documentation's behavior when you write code, but when the API disagrees with its docs, the API wins.

Using your API key

Yes, send it. It's in the docs, it costs nothing, and if NASA starts enforcing rate limits on this endpoint, you'll be covered. I honestly can't tell whether this endpoint checks the key at all: our requests without a key have worked fine. But there's no downside to including it.

Update fetchPictures:

const API_KEY = 'YOUR_KEY_HERE';

export async function fetchPictures(): Promise<ApodPicture[]> {
  const response = await axios.get<RawApodEntry[]>(BASE_URL, {
    params: { api_key: API_KEY },
  });
  return response.data.map(toPicture);
}

The params object is the same pattern you used with the old API. Axios builds ?api_key=... onto the URL for you.

A fix the new docs reveal: media_type can be iframe

The documentation you pasted says media_type can be "image, video, or iframe." Your adapter only treats 'video' as a video, so an iframe entry would be treated as an image. It would then fail to load, because there's no image file. Update the first line of toPicture:

const isVideo = raw.media_type === 'video' || raw.media_type === 'iframe';

findVideoUrl already searches for <iframe> tags, so these entries will embed correctly in the detail view, the same way your two videos now do.

That's a good example of why reading updated docs closely matters, even when they're not fully accurate. The parameter list was wrong in practice, but this field description was useful.

Technically yes, but it would make the app worse, so I wouldn't do it.

Three years is about 1,095 days. Minus the 25 from the list endpoint, that's around 1,070 individual requests every time someone opens the site without a cache. Here's what that costs:

Load time. Each single-day response includes the full basic_html page, around 20–40 KB, so 1,070 of them is roughly 20–40 MB of downloads before anything appears. Browsers also limit how many requests run at once to the same server, so they would queue up. Depending on the connection, the "Loading..." message could sit there for many seconds, possibly minutes. Your grader opens the site, sees nothing, and that's what they remember.

Getting blocked. The endpoint has no documented rate limit, but firing a thousand requests in a burst is exactly the pattern servers throttle or block. The legacy NASA API allowed 1,000 requests per hour per key; if anything like that applies here, a single page load would use it all up. If NASA starts rejecting requests mid-load, your app ends up with gaps or nothing at all, and possibly in the middle of your demo video.

Being a good API citizen. The assignment explicitly asks you to think about rate limits. Downloading three years of data that a visitor will mostly never scroll to is the opposite of what it's asking for.

Diminishing returns. Nothing in the rubric gets better with more data. Searching, sorting, filtering, and Previous/Next work identically with 60 entries or 1,000.

Estimating feasibility of fetching a year's worth of data.

Estimating feasibility of fetching a year's worth of data.

Done

A year is much more reasonable than three, but loading it the same way we load 60 days would still cause problems. It works if you change how you load.

The numbers

Requests: about 365 days minus 25 from the list endpoint, so around 340 individual requests.

Download size: at roughly 20–40 KB each, that's 7–14 MB, a third of the three-year figure.

Cache size: after conversion, each picture is mostly its explanation text, around 1–2 KB. A year of pictures is well under 1 MB, which fits easily in browser storage.

Why the current approach doesn't scale to this

Right now, fetchPictures fires every request at once and shows nothing until all of them finish. With 340 requests, that means:

A long blank wait. The user sees "Loading..." until the slowest of 340 requests comes back.

A burst of 340 simultaneous requests. That's the pattern most likely to get throttled.

How to make a year work well

Three changes would make it practical:

Show the first page immediately. Display the latest 25 as soon as the list endpoint answers, so the app is usable within a second. Then keep loading older days in the background, adding them to the list as they arrive. The search, sort, and filters keep working the whole time over whatever has loaded so far.

Fetch in small batches. Instead of 340 requests at once, send them 10 at a time, waiting for each batch to finish before starting the next. It takes a little longer overall, but it's polite to NASA's server and far less likely to be blocked.

Cache in localStorage, with an expiry. Unlike sessionStorage, localStorage survives closing the browser, so a returning visitor (or your grader on a second visit) loads instantly. A timestamp stored next to the data lets you refetch after a day, so new pictures still appear.

The tricky part is the first change. fetchPictures can no longer just return a finished array, because the data arrives over time. Instead, App would pass in a callback, a function that fetchPictures calls each time a batch arrives, which adds the new pictures to state. It's a good pattern to learn, but it touches App.tsx and api/apod.ts, and it adds a "still loading older pictures" indicator to the UI.

That's the cache from Step 19 doing exactly what it was built for. On refresh, fetchPictures finds the 60 pictures saved in sessionStorage and returns them right away, without ever contacting NASA. So your new totalDays value never gets used. Refreshing doesn't clear sessionStorage; only closing the tab does.

There may also be a second cause, depending on where you changed the number.

Check 1: Which totalDays did you change?

After the caching step, there are two functions with a totalDays = 60 default:

async function fetchFromNasa(totalDays = 60) { ... }          // inner function
export async function fetchPictures(totalDays = 60) { ... }   // the one App calls

App calls fetchPictures() with no argument, so fetchPictures's default is the one that applies. It passes its own value down to fetchFromNasa, so changing only fetchFromNasa's default has no effect. Make sure you changed the number in fetchPictures.

Check 2: Clear the old cache

To see the new number right now, do either of these:

Open the site in a new tab. A new tab starts with an empty sessionStorage.

Clear it in DevTools: open DevTools, go to the Application tab (in Safari, Storage), expand Session Storage, click your site, right-click the apod-pictures entry, and delete it. Then refresh.

The permanent fix: include the size in the cache key

Rather than clearing the cache by hand every time you change the number, make the key depend on totalDays. In fetchPictures, replace the CACHE_KEY constant with a key built from it:

export async function fetchPictures(totalDays = 60): Promise<ApodPicture[]> {
  const cacheKey = `apod-pictures-${totalDays}`;

  const cached = sessionStorage.getItem(cacheKey);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached) as ApodPicture[];

  const pictures = await fetchFromNasa(totalDays);
  sessionStorage.setItem(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(pictures));
  return pictures;
}

Delete the old const CACHE_KEY = 'apod-pictures'; line too.

Now 60 days is cached under apod-pictures-60 and 90 days under apod-pictures-90. Changing the number means a different key, which has nothing saved under it yet, so the app fetches fresh. This is called cache invalidation: making sure a cache never serves data that no longer matches the request. It's famously one of the trickiest problems in programming, and you just ran into a textbook case of it.

Test

Change totalDays in fetchPictures to, say, 90, save, and refresh. The List should grow to about 90 entries.

Refresh again. It should load instantly from the cache, with no new apod-basic requests in the Network tab.

Remember the request count grows with the number. 90 days means 65 single-day requests on the first load, which is fine; a few hundred would bring back the problems we just discussed. Then run npm run build, commit, and push.
